summary: Specifies how SIP interworks with QSIG, a signalling protocol for circuit-switched calls inside corporate private telephone networks. It lets calls and features cross between the two worlds. It is a Best Current Practice document.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator between two phone languages so an office phone system and an Internet phone system can understand each other.

questions: how does sip interwork with qsig
what is a sip qsig gateway
how are qsig cause values mapped to sip responses
subtitle: How a gateway turns circuit-switched QSIG phone signalling into SIP calls, and back, inside a company network.

tldr.problem: Corporate phone systems built on circuit-switched QSIG are moving to SIP, and for years the two will coexist, so calls must be able to cross between them.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway looks like a PINX (private exchange) to the QSIG side and like a SIP user agent to the IP side. It maps QSIG messages to SIP messages and back, maps phone numbers to URIs, and connects the media streams to the bearer channels.
tldr.outcome: The RFC covers basic calls only: speech, DTMF, facsimile and modem media. Supplementary services such as call transfer are left for future work. It is a Best Current Practice and has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4497 is a Best Current Practice and has been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Interwork SIP and QSIG
sections.content:
QSIG is a signalling protocol that runs between Private Integrated Services eXchanges (PINX, the formal name for a PBX) in a Private Integrated Services Network (PISN). It sets up and clears circuit-switched calls, mainly telephone calls. It is specified in Ecma Standards that are also published as ISO/IEC standards. The name comes from its use at the Q reference point, the demarcation between two PINXs.

SIP is an application-layer protocol for creating, modifying and ending multimedia sessions, and a telephone call is just a session with audio. As corporate telephony moves from circuit switching to Internet technology, the two will coexist, perhaps for several years. Gateways that translate between them make calls possible between a QSIG user and a SIP user.

This RFC covers signalling for basic services: a two-way transfer path for speech, DTMF, facsimile and modem media. It does not cover supplementary services such as call transfer and call diversion, nor interworking with a public IP network, though the RFC says the same functions could in principle apply there.
sections.plainLanguage: Old office phones and new Internet phones need to call each other while both are still in use. A translator lets them talk.

sections.title: Gateway Architecture
sections.content:
Corporate voice networks adopted ISDN-like technology in the 1980s. PINXs are linked by digital transmission that carries voice in fixed-rate channels, typically 64 Kbit/s, with signalling in a separate channel. A typical arrangement is a T1 or E1 link with a 64 Kbit/s signalling channel and 23 or 30 bearer channels. The signalling channel plus its bearer channels form an inter-PINX link.

The gateway appears as a PINX to other PINXs and as a SIP endpoint to other SIP entities. Besides the signalling interworking function, the RFC assumes it has physical interfaces on both sides and a way to packetize media toward the IP network and de-packetize it coming back. On the IP side, UDP and TCP carry SIP, with TLS and SCTP optional.

The gateway keeps an association between each QSIG call and a SIP dialog. A QSIG SETUP triggers a SIP INVITE, and a SIP INVITE triggers a QSIG SETUP. The RFC also notes that a SIP network can interconnect different parts of a PISN through two gateways. Carrying QSIG inside SIP messages is out of scope.

Conformance is straightforward: the gateway SHALL support QSIG as a gateway and SIP as a user agent (RFC 3261), reliable provisional responses (RFC 3262), and SDP used with the offer/answer model (RFC 3264). The Privacy and P-Asserted-Identity headers are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway is a double agent. To the office phones it acts like another office phone exchange, and to the Internet phones it acts like another Internet phone.

sections.title: Setting Up Calls in Each Direction
sections.content:
QSIG to SIP. A QSIG SETUP with a complete called number becomes a SIP INVITE, and the gateway also sends a QSIG CALL PROCEEDING. The INVITE carries a Supported header with option tag 100rel and an SDP offer. A SIP 100 response triggers nothing. A 180 maps to a QSIG ALERTING. A 181, 182 or 183 maps to a QSIG PROGRESS. The first SIP 2xx maps to a QSIG CONNECT, and the gateway sends the SIP ACK.

SIP to QSIG. A SIP INVITE for a new call becomes a QSIG SETUP, if a suitable channel is free. If none is, the gateway sends SIP 503 (Service Unavailable). QSIG ALERTING maps to SIP 180, PROGRESS to 183, and CONNECT to 200 OK, after which the gateway sends a QSIG CONNECT ACKNOWLEDGE. SDP is placed in these responses according to whether reliable provisional responses are in use and whether an offer has already been made.

Overlap signalling. QSIG can send a number digit by digit, but SIP sends it all at once (en bloc). The RFC strongly recommends avoiding overlap in the SIP network, and a gateway SHOULD convert overlap to en bloc using timers, numbering plan information or a Sending Complete element. Only when that is impossible does the gateway send new INVITEs with more digits, following RFC 3578.

Early media matters here. When QSIG signals progress description number 1 or 8, the gateway connects the media streams to the bearer channel, so the caller can hear ringback tones or announcements before the call is answered.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone dials, the translator turns the dialing message into the other language, passes along 'ringing' and 'answered' news, and joins the sound paths so both people can hear each other.

sections.title: Clearing Calls and Failures
sections.content:
The RFC says a QSIG DISCONNECT, RELEASE or RELEASE COMPLETE is handled according to how far the call got. After the call is established the gateway sends a SIP BYE. If it has sent an INVITE and only seen provisional responses, it sends CANCEL. If it has not yet answered a received INVITE, it sends a final response chosen from a table of QSIG cause values. The default is 500.

In the other direction, a SIP BYE or CANCEL becomes a QSIG DISCONNECT with cause value 16 (normal call clearing). A SIP 4xx, 5xx or 6xx final response to an INVITE becomes a DISCONNECT with a cause value from a second table, unless the gateway can retry, for example by supplying credentials after a 401 or 407. The default cause is 31 (normal, unspecified).

If either side hits a timer expiry or protocol error that clears its call, the gateway clears the other side too. Errors are not forwarded as such. A request to change media in a way the PISN bearer cannot support is refused with SIP 488 (Not Acceptable Here).
sections.plainLanguage: When one person hangs up or something goes wrong, the translator tells the other side in a way it understands, like turning a busy signal into the right kind of 'line busy' message.

sections.title: Mapping Numbers and Identities
sections.content:
QSIG identifies users by numbers in the Called party number, Calling party number and Connected number information elements. The latter two carry a presentation indicator (which can say privacy is required) and a screening indicator. SIP uses URIs in the Request-URI, From and To headers, optionally the P-Asserted-Identity header (RFC 3325), and the Privacy header (RFC 3323). The method for converting between numbers and URIs is outside the scope of the RFC.

QSIG to SIP. The called number becomes a URI in both the Request-URI and the To header. For the calling number, if a URI is derived and presentation is allowed, the gateway puts it in From and in P-Asserted-Identity where supported. If presentation is restricted, it uses an anonymous From and a Privacy header with priv-value set to id. If no URI can be derived, the From header identifies the gateway itself.

SIP to QSIG. The Request-URI, not the To header, becomes the called number, because re-targeting can change the Request-URI while leaving To alone. For the calling number the gateway prefers a verified signed message/sipfrag body or a trusted P-Asserted-Identity, marking the screening indicator "network provided". By default it SHOULD NOT use an unsigned, unvalidated From header, since that comes from an untrusted source, though a gateway MAY be configured to do so, marking it "user provided, not screened".
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number is like a name tag. The translator rewrites each name tag into the other language and respects 'please keep my name private' requests.

sections.title: Basic Services and Media
sections.content:
The gateway builds the QSIG Bearer capability element from the SDP offer in the INVITE. If there is no offer or the only media type is audio, it uses a fixed encoding: CCITT standardized coding, "3,1 kHz audio", circuit mode and 64 Kbits/s, with the user information layer 1 protocol set to G.711 mu-law or A-law depending on the PISN.

Going the other way, the SDP offer is derived from the QSIG Bearer capability element, where "speech" and "3,1 kHz audio" both map to media type audio. Mappings from Low or High layer compatibility elements are left out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator picks the right kind of sound line on each side, so a voice call stays a voice call.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Normal SIP security applies (Digest authentication, TLS, S/MIME). Translating between the two worlds adds specific risks, and the RFC lists them:

  • Restricted numbers: a SIP user can create a Request-URI that a PISN user would be barred from dialling, so administrators may want policies on which URIs are allowed through.
  • Response code abuse: a SIP endpoint can pick the response code and so influence the QSIG cause value, though this is unlikely to enable fraud. Administrators may want to adjust the mapping.
  • From and To headers: they are not policed, so an unverified From should be used for the calling number only if the originator is authenticated and authorized to assert it.
  • Early media: cut-through before answer lets the called side play audio for an indefinite time. The RFC judges the usefulness to outweigh the risk, but suggests a switch or time limit.
  • Denial of service: a SIP agent could launch 100 simultaneous INVITEs at a 100-port gateway, so limits per authenticated source are suggested.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator can be tricked, so it should check who is really calling, not let one caller hog all the phone lines, and limit free sounds before answering.
